content: The United Republic of Tanzania, where HIV is endemic, serves as an ideal setting to evaluate optimal cervical cancer screening strategies for women living with HIV. For the baseline analysis, it was assumed that 70% of women attended each routine screening event, and 90% complied with follow-up care. Outcomes were assessed over the lifetime of birth cohorts eligible for screening from 2030 onwards. These outcomes included cervical cancer incidence and mortality, pre-cancer treatments, additional preterm deliveries due to pre-cancer treatment, and cost-effectiveness. Various sensitivity analyses, including probabilistic sensitivity analysis for cost-effectiveness, were conducted. A systematic review of studies was performed to address the values and preferences of end-users, healthcare providers, and other stakeholders. The literature was organized by study design, methodology, location, and population, and presented to the Guideline Development Group (GDG). An anonymous, voluntary survey was distributed to women and girls aged 15 years and older, regardless of their prior cervical cancer screening or treatment status. The survey, approved by the WHO Ethics Review Committee, was conducted in English and French from June 22 to September 18, 2020. Awareness of the survey was raised through webinars and promoted via organizations such as the Union for International Cancer Control and WHO advisory groups. Responses from 561 participants, including qualitative feedback, were analyzed. To assess the feasibility, acceptability, resource needs, and equity considerations of implementing priority algorithms, a survey of GDG members was conducted using the Context and Implementation of Complex Interventions (CICI) framework. GDG members were asked to evaluate the sustainability of each algorithm in achieving large-scale cervical cancer elimination goals. Specific components of cervical cancer screening and management, such as demand generation, access to screening, follow-up management, workforce training, infrastructure development, registry maintenance, and integration with other health services, were assessed. The perspectives of eight stakeholder groups, including national and regional health authorities, professional societies, healthcare providers, community health workers, clients, and the community, were considered. The GDG meetings to formulate recommendations were held virtually. Evidence-to-decision (EtD) tables summarizing evidence, values, preferences, resource use, feasibility, equity, and acceptability were prepared and shared with GDG members before each meeting. These tables were discussed during the meetings, and members provided input via email. Recommendations were finalized through consensus, with strong recommendations made when the benefits of an intervention clearly outweighed the harms, and conditional recommendations made when the benefits likely outweighed the harms in most settings. The WHO recommendations aim to improve cervical cancer screening coverage and outcomes, set quality standards, and reduce cervical cancer mortality. Transition strategies may be required to move from existing screening infrastructure to the recommended approaches. WHO plans to publish stepwise implementation guidelines to support countries in selecting and scaling up algorithms. A multidisciplinary health ministry team should select screening algorithms based on available resources, feasibility, and acceptability. Decisions about follow-up care and contact timing are also necessary. The guideline distinguishes between three clinical scenarios in routine screening programs: regular screening intervals, follow-up of women with a positive primary screening test but negative triage test, and follow-up after treatment. Cervical cancer screening and treatment should also be provided to transgender men, non-binary individuals, and intersex individuals with a cervix. More data on screening and treatment for these populations, including those living with HIV, are needed. Healthcare systems should be inclusive of these groups, requiring additional training and sensitization of health workers. Public health authorities should prioritize awareness and access to cervical cancer screening and treatment for these populations. High-risk HPV DNA tests are recommended as primary screening tests due to their ability to identify carcinogenic HPV genotypes. Self-sampling or provider sampling can be used for HPV DNA testing. Cytology tests, such as Pap smears and liquid-based cytology, identify atypical cervical cells but require trained experts and sophisticated processing. Visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) is not suitable for postmenopausal women or when the transformation zone is not visible. Colposcopy may be used for further evaluation or to guide treatment decisions. In a screen-and-treat approach, women who test positive are treated without histological diagnosis. Ablative treatments destroy abnormal cervical tissue but do not provide a tissue specimen for evaluation. Excisional treatments, such as LLETZ, remove the transformation zone and provide a specimen for pathology. The guideline includes 23 recommendations and 7 good practice statements on cervical cancer screening and treatment. Among these, 6 recommendations and 3 good practice statements are identical for the general population and women living with HIV, while others are specific to each group. WHO recommends starting regular cervical cancer screening at age 30, prioritizing women aged 30–49, and using HPV DNA testing as the primary screening method. Screening intervals of 5–10 years are suggested, depending on resources and feasibility. The recommendations emphasize the importance of population-based screening and treatment strategies to reduce cervical cancer mortality. WHO plans to issue additional recommendations and stepwise implementation guidelines to support countries in achieving cervical cancer elimination goals.
